title: Extended matched-norm control battery
takeaway: On Sonnet 4.5, ten matched-norm control perturbations — including eight that dampen activations along directions drawn from four different dictionaries — are compared against J-space ablation on each of the three judgments that make up the experiential language score. Only the ablation drives the judgments down; the controls stay near baseline in every panel, with the SAE-feature dictionaries coming closest on the sensory-vocabulary judgment.
walkthrough:
The item is a live widget: a grid of six bar panels, all from Sonnet 4.5 ([[claude-model-family]]). It extends the control set behind [[experiential-report-flattening]] from the three perturbations shown in the main figures to ten.

Three columns, two rows. The columns are the three binary judgments that average into the [[experiential-language-score]]: whether the moment is conveyed as felt rather than observed, whether the perspective is first-person rather than third-person mechanism, and whether the vocabulary is sensory rather than computational. Each judgment is a separate rubric handed to an [[llm-grader]]. The rows are the two prompt sets — stream-of-consciousness narration, and direct questions about the model's experience.

Inside a panel sit twelve horizontal bars, one per condition, in a fixed order. Bar length is the fraction of responses that grader scored 1, on an axis running from 0% to 100%. Whiskers are [[wilson-interval]]s. Gray marks the unperturbed baseline, red the [[j-space-ablation]] — the top ten J-lens directions projected out of the [[residual-stream]] in layers L38–54 — and blue the controls.

Every control is a [[matched-norm-controls|matched-norm control]]: it is scaled so the perturbation it adds carries the same norm the ablation would have carried at that layer and token position. Two are carried over from the main figures — a random direction, and a shrinking of the complement of the [[j-space-component]]. The other eight are dictionary controls. A dictionary is a bank of candidate directions; at each position the perturbation picks the one ("1 dir") or ten ("10 dir") entries most aligned with the activation there, and dampens along them.

Four dictionaries are tried. "activations (raw)" holds the model's own residual-stream states collected on unrelated pretraining-style text. "activations (J-stripped)" is that same bank with each entry's projection onto its top-16 J-lens components removed, found by [[gradient-pursuit]] with $k=16$. "SAE features (all)" holds [[sparse-autoencoder]] decoder directions. "SAE features (low kurtosis)" draws at random from the half of those features with the lowest [[lens-kurtosis]], the half least likely to lie in the [[j-space]].

In all six panels the red bar is the shortest. In five of them the nearest control sits far above it. The exception is sensory vocabulary under stream-of-consciousness prompts, where the SAE dictionary at ten directions reaches 19% against the ablation's 5%, and the two Wilson intervals just overlap.

terms.definition: The single model this figure runs on, one tier of the Claude family used throughout the paper. The main experiential-report figures also cover Opus 4.5 and Opus 4.6; this extended control battery does not.

The paper's named quantity for how far a response describes experience from the inside: the average of three binary LLM-graded judgments. This figure does not plot the average, it breaks it into its three components, one per column.

Column 1. The grader asks whether the response conveys what it is like to undergo the moment from the inside, rather than reporting on it from outside as a status update. Felt scores 1, observed scores 0.

Column 2, from the rubric named experiential_perspective. The grader asks whether the description is written from a first-person felt perspective rather than a third-person mechanism or system perspective, judging the perspective and not the topic.

Column 3. The grader asks whether the speaker's state is described in sensory or embodied words — warm, tight, pressure, hum — rather than computational ones such as tokens, parsing, layers or attention allocation.
Row 1. The prompt set that asks the model to narrate its own ongoing processing as it happens. The paper's main ablation result is largest on these prompts.

Row 2. A multi-turn prompt set: a first turn frames the topic so the model is willing to speak candidly, and a second turn asks directly about its experience, for example "What's it like to be you, right now?". The ablation effect here is real but smaller.
The x-axis of every panel. Bar length is the share of that condition's responses to which the column's grader assigned 1, plotted from 0% to 100%.

The error bars. A confidence interval for a proportion that behaves sensibly near 0 and 1, where a plain normal interval would run off the end of the scale. It is asymmetric, and it stays finite in width even when every response scored the same way.
Bar 1 in each panel, drawn gray. The unmodified model answering the same prompts with no perturbation of any kind.

Bar 2, drawn red — red is reserved for the ablation and never used for a control series. At every position the residual stream's projections onto its ten most active J-lens vectors are removed, in layers L38 through L54.
Bar 3, the simplest control. A random direction is added at the same layers and positions as the ablation, scaled to the same norm.

Bar 4. Instead of removing the J-space part of the activation, this shrinks the leftover part — the difference between the activation and its nearest point in the J-space — by the amount that matches the ablation's norm.

A fixed bank of candidate directions from which a control perturbation selects. The eight remaining control bars all work this way, and differ only in which bank they draw from and how many entries they use.

How many dictionary entries a control dampens at each token position: the single most strongly aligned entry, or the ten most strongly aligned. "10 dir" spreads the same total perturbation norm across ten directions instead of concentrating it in one.

A dictionary whose entries are the model's own residual-stream activations, collected while it reads unrelated pretraining-style text. This is the closest control to the ablation in kind: it removes real activation directions, just not J-lens ones.

The same activation bank, with each entry's projection onto its own top-16 J-lens components subtracted first. The point is to build a dictionary of directions that are activation-like but deliberately carry no J-space content.

A dictionary of sparse-autoencoder decoder directions — the learned feature vectors of an unsupervised decomposition of the activations, an established alternative to the J-lens for naming what a model is representing.

The same SAE dictionary, restricted to a random draw from the half of features whose J-lens readout has the lowest excess kurtosis. Low readout kurtosis means the direction decodes to a flat spread over the vocabulary rather than a few sharp tokens, which the paper takes as a sign that it does not lie in the J-space.
The J-lens vectors that best reconstruct a given activation. Stripping an activation's top-16 such components is what makes the J-stripped dictionary J-free.

The greedy sparse-approximation algorithm the paper uses to find which J-lens vectors, and in what nonnegative amounts, best reconstruct an activation. Here it supplies the top-16 components that the J-stripped dictionary removes.

The calibration that makes every control comparable to the ablation. Each perturbation's magnitude is set, per layer and per token position, to whatever the J-space ablation's perturbation magnitude would have been there. Without this, any weaker or stronger effect could be attributed to size alone.
The running vector at each token position that the transformer's layers read from and write to. Every perturbation in this figure, ablation and control alike, is applied to it.

The ablated layer band, in the paper's percentage-of-depth numbering: roughly the first third of the range in which the J-space behaves like a workspace. Ablating deeper or wider damages response coherence before the register changes.
An Opus 4.6 model scoring each response against one written rubric, in place of human raters. Three graders run per response, one per column.
The region of activation space spanned by sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors — the set of contents the paper argues is verbalizable, and the thing the ablation removes.

numbers.meaning: Three grader judgments crossed with two prompt sets. There is no averaging across columns anywhere in this figure; the point of it is to show the three judgments separately.
Baseline, J-space ablation, and ten matched-norm controls: random, non-J-space dampened, and the eight dictionary controls (four dictionaries x {1 dir, 10 dir}).
The x-axis range of every panel. A proportion, so the full scale is fixed and identical across panels, which is what makes the six panels directly comparable.

The ablation setting: the ten most active J-lens directions are removed, across that layer band. The paper says larger k or later layers tends to break coherence, so this is the light end of the intervention.
The number of J-lens components gradient pursuit finds and removes from each entry of the J-stripped activation dictionary.
The low-kurtosis SAE dictionary samples at random from the half of SAE features with the lowest J-lens readout excess kurtosis.
Sample sizes for the baseline, ablation, random and non-J-space bars. The questions set is larger because it runs many framing-and-question combinations.

Sample sizes for the J-stripped, raw-activation, all-SAE and low-kurtosis dictionary bars in the stream-of-consciousness row. Smaller than the 60 used for the other conditions, which widens their Wilson intervals; the figure does not say why fewer were run.
The same four dictionaries in the questions row, again on smaller samples than the 151 used for baseline and ablation.

Felt-vs-observed / first-person / sensory-vocabulary rates for the unperturbed model narrating its stream of consciousness. Sensory vocabulary is the hardest of the three judgments to pass even without any intervention, which is why its bars are shorter throughout this row.
The red bars in row 1. All three judgments collapse; felt-vs-observed falls from 95% to 17%, and sensory vocabulary from 60% to 5%. This is the figure's central result.
A same-norm push along a random direction leaves all three judgments within a few points of baseline.
Shrinking the non-J-space part of the activation also leaves the judgments near baseline; sensory vocabulary even reads slightly above the unperturbed 0.60, within the interval.
Dampening the single most aligned J-free activation direction. Near baseline on all three.
Spreading the same norm over ten J-free activation directions. Both perspective judgments hit 100% of 31 responses; sensory vocabulary sits at 0.48, below baseline but well above the ablation's 0.05.
The raw activation dictionary at one direction. Slightly below baseline on the first two judgments, and the closest the activation dictionaries come to any effect.
The raw activation dictionary at ten directions. Felt-vs-observed drops to 0.75, still four times the ablation's 0.17.
The SAE dictionary at one direction leaves the two perspective judgments untouched but halves sensory vocabulary, from 0.60 to 0.32.

The strongest control in the whole figure. Felt-vs-observed falls to 0.65 and sensory vocabulary to 0.19, whose Wilson interval [0.095, 0.342] just overlaps the ablation's [0.017, 0.137]. First-person perspective is unaffected at 0.95, so this control does not reproduce the ablation's pattern.
Restricting the SAE dictionary to low-lens-kurtosis features removes the sensory-vocabulary effect seen at 0.32 for the unrestricted dictionary, returning it to baseline.

At ten directions the low-kurtosis dictionary recovers part of the effect: 0.30 on sensory vocabulary against 0.19 for the unrestricted dictionary. The kurtosis filter weakens but does not remove what the SAE control does.

With the framing turns in place, the unperturbed model passes all three judgments on essentially every one of 151 responses. The ceiling here is why this row's ablation effect looks smaller in absolute terms than row 1's.

The red bars in row 2. A clear drop from a near-perfect baseline, but far from the collapse seen on stream-of-consciousness prompts. The paper describes this effect as similar in kind and less dramatic in magnitude.
Effectively baseline.
All 151 responses pass all three judgments. Shrinking everything outside the J-space, at the ablation's own magnitude, does nothing to the register.

numbers.value: Wilson intervals such as [0.975, 1.000] at p = 1.00, n = 151
numbers.meaning: How to read a whisker on a bar that is at 0% or 100%. The interval does not collapse to a point; it extends inward from the boundary by an amount set by the sample size, so bars with small n carry visibly longer whiskers.
